opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we went through the remaining failures on SWE-bench Verified, they fell into a few buckets. The first thing worth saying is that some of them aren't really model failures at all. Even after the Verified filtering, there are tasks where the hidden tests check for something pretty specific: an exact error message string, a particular function name, or a behavior the issue never really specified. A strong engineer reading only the issue could write a perfectly reasonable fix and still fail those tests. So some fraction of the remaining problems are closer to underspecified than hard, and I wouldn't expect anyone to get to a true 100%.

Of the ones that are genuinely hard, the pattern I noticed most is that the model gets the localization right. It finds the right file and the right function, but it fixes the symptom rather than the root cause. It patches the one code path in the bug report, when the real fix belongs a layer down, or the same bug shows up in three sibling places. A senior engineer on that codebase would know about those because they have context on how the library is supposed to work. The agent is building that understanding from scratch every time, in a limited number of steps.

Another big category is verification. The agents that do well are the ones that write a reproduction script first, confirm they can trigger the bug, make the fix, and then confirm the fix works and nothing else broke. On the harder problems, the model sometimes can't build a good reproduction. Maybe the environment is tricky, or the bug only shows up in some edge configuration. Without that feedback loop, it's guessing, and it tends to declare victory too early. A lot of our progress came from getting the model to be more skeptical of itself and keep testing instead of stopping when the first thing looks plausible.

And then there's a long tail of problems that need real domain knowledge: numerical precision stuff in scientific libraries, subtle semantics in something like SymPy, or Django ORM internals. The model often knows the general area but not the deep invariants a maintainer has internalized.

So my overall take is that the frontier is moving away from "can the model write the code" toward "can the model build an accurate mental model of an unfamiliar system and check its own work." Those are exactly the skills that matter for real-world software engineering too, which is why I still think the benchmark is useful even as the numbers get high. The remaining problems are a pretty good map of what separates a decent engineer from a really good one.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes tasks that are underspecified and may fail reasonable fixes from genuinely hard tasks, addressing whether the remaining failures stem from problem descriptions or agent capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that a big chunk of what's left isn't really "hard" in the way people imagine. When we dug into the problems that the agents were consistently failing, a lot of them were basically unfair in one way or another. The issue description is underspecified, so there are multiple reasonable fixes, but the hidden tests only accept the one the original maintainer happened to write. Or the test is checking for a specific exception message string, and there's no way you could guess that from the issue. Or the fix depends on some convention in the repo that's only in a maintainer's head. A human engineer dropped into that codebase cold would fail those too. So I'd actually say the ceiling on SWE-bench Verified is meaningfully below 100%, and we're closer to it than the raw number suggests.

That said, there is a real residual set that I find more interesting. Those tend to be problems where the fix requires understanding a lot of the codebase at once. Not just reading a few files, but holding a mental model of how a dozen components interact, and realizing the bug is in a place the issue never mentions. Models are still a bit too local. They find something that looks plausibly wrong near the stack trace and patch it, and the patch is even correct in isolation, but it's not the actual root cause. A senior engineer has this instinct of "wait, this doesn't smell right, let me keep digging," and models are more inclined to declare victory early.

The other failure mode I'd call out is verification. The models that do best aren't necessarily smarter at writing the patch. They're better at writing a reproduction, running it, and actually believing the result rather than their own prior. When you watch the trajectories, a lot of failures are the model making a change, running tests that don't actually exercise the change, and saying "great, done." So part of what remains is less a capability gap and more a discipline gap, and that's something you can train pretty directly.

And then honestly, I think we're near the point where the benchmark stops being the right question. Once you're in the high eighties, the remaining delta is mostly noise and benchmark artifacts. The thing we actually care about is whether the model can do a multi-day task in a real repo with real ambiguity, where it has to ask a clarifying question or push back on a bad spec. SWE-bench doesn't measure any of that. So I'd rather we spent our energy on what comes after it than squeezing out the last few points.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes tasks that exceed agents’ capabilities from tasks that are unfair or underspecified because their descriptions do not reveal what the hidden tests expect.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate problems where the model can’t figure out the fix from problems where it can’t get the feedback it needs. An agent might have a reasonable hypothesis, but if it can’t reproduce the bug, get the environment running, or run the relevant tests, it’s hard to know whether it’s making progress.

Then there are problems where the actual patch is small, but finding it requires understanding how several parts of a large codebase interact. That’s a different challenge from writing code. You have to build a hypothesis, investigate it, and revise it when the evidence doesn’t fit.

So I wouldn’t assume the remaining problems are all beyond the models’ reach in some fundamental sense. Some need better tooling and feedback; others need better reasoning over a long investigation. The interesting question is where the agent gets stuck, rather than just whether it ultimately passes the test.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the remaining tasks are fundamentally beyond models’ reach, but attributes difficulty to tooling, feedback, and long investigations. It does not raise the possibility that tasks are impossible because of their problem descriptions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what’s actually blocking the agent. Is it missing some capability, or is it failing to find the right information? Those can look very similar in a benchmark score, but they suggest pretty different things to work on.

A repository gives you this enormous space to search. You have to figure out which code matters, understand the intended behavior, make a change, and then get useful feedback about whether that change worked. An agent can be quite good at writing the patch once it has the right context and still fail the overall task because it went down the wrong path early on.

So I’d be careful about treating the remaining problems as a clean boundary of what models can reason about. Some may require better reasoning, but others may require better tools, better feedback, or more effective use of time. I’d want to look at the individual failures and ask: if you gave the agent one useful hint, would it finish? That tells you a lot more about what’s missing than the aggregate score does.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether failures stem from missing capability or failure to find the right information, but it does not ask whether tasks are impossible because of their problem descriptions.
